lines.en: It has long been assumed that memory works like a recording, yet recent research suggests otherwise.
The study, the findings of which were published last year, challenges everything we thought we knew.
What the data demonstrate is not that the method fails, but that its success depends on conditions we rarely meet.
It is essential that every participant be informed of the risks before the experiment begins.
However convincing a theory may appear, it must be abandoned when the evidence turns against it.
Not until the experiment had been repeated forty times did the journal agree to publish the results.
The conclusion, far from being certain, is little more than a well-supported hypothesis.
Were the sample larger, the findings would carry considerably more weight.
What remains unclear is whether the effect exists outside the laboratory.
Rarely does a single paper change a whole field, but when it does, textbooks are rewritten.
The hypothesis, attractive though it is, rests on data collected from only three hospitals.
What the committee questioned was not the result itself, but the method by which it had been reached.
It is customary in academic writing to cite every source, however small its contribution may seem.

The paper argues, with some justification, that earlier studies had confused correlation with cause.
